questions.title: How exactly does the partition function cancel when deriving the DPO likelihood from Bradley–Terry?
questions.question_body:
In the paper, the optimal KL-regularized policy is written as

\[ \pi_r(y\mid x) = \frac{1}{Z(x)}\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\,\exp\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)\right), \]

so that

\[ r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi_r(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)} + \beta \log Z(x). \]

Bradley–Terry gives preference probabilities as

\[ p(y_1 \succ y_2 \mid x) = \sigma\big(r(x,y_1) - r(x,y_2)\big). \]

The paper says the partition term \(\beta\log Z(x)\) cancels when you substitute the reparameterized \(r\) into this BT model, yielding a loss entirely in terms of \(\pi_\theta\) and \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\). Could someone show this cancellation step-by-step, starting from the two equations above and ending at

\[ p(y_1 \succ y_2 \mid x)=\sigma\!\left( \beta\log \tfrac{\pi(y_1\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_1\mid x)} - \beta\log \tfrac{\pi(y_2\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_2\mid x)} \right)? \]

I want to be sure I’m not missing any hidden assumptions about sequence lengths or tokenization.

questions.title: What exactly is the role of the hyperparameter \(\beta\) in DPO, and how do I pick it to target a desired KL?
questions.question_body:
In DPO, the objective for a pair \((y_w, y_l)\) is

\[ \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\log \sigma\!\left( \beta\log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta\log \tfrac{\pi_{\theta}(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)} \right). \]

Theoretically \(\beta\) is the Lagrange multiplier from the KL-regularized RL objective, but practically: 
- How does \(\beta\) trade off reward maximization vs. closeness to \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)? 
- Is there a principled way to set \(\beta\) to achieve a target sequence-level KL \(\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_\theta\,\Vert\,\pi_{\text{ref}})\)? 
- What happens if I rescale an underlying reward by a constant factor (e.g., annotator calibration shifts). Does \(\beta\) absorb that, or do I need to retune it?

questions.title: Why can DPO outperform PPO even when PPO has access to the ground-truth reward?
questions.question_body:
In the sentiment experiment, the paper reports that DPO’s reward/KL frontier dominates PPO even when PPO uses the ground-truth reward ("PPO-GT"). If both optimize the same KL-regularized objective,

\[ \max_{\pi} \; \mathbb{E}_{y\sim \pi(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,y)] - \beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi\,\Vert\,\pi_{\text{ref}}), \]

why is PPO-GT still worse in practice? Is it due to sampling variance, value/baseline estimation error, credit assignment over long sequences, or something specific to language modeling (e.g., exposure bias)? Any intuition or empirical diagnostics would help reconcile this.

questions.title: Is DPO just supervised fine-tuning on preferred responses? How exactly does it differ from MLE or unlikelihood?
questions.question_body:
Naively, DPO looks like it increases \(\log \pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)\) and decreases \(\log \pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)\), similar to a combination of MLE on \(y_w\) and unlikelihood on \(y_l\). But the DPO loss weighs examples via a logistic term on the implicit reward difference:

\[ \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\text{DPO}} = -\beta\,\mathbb{E}\left[ \sigma\big(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l) - \hat r_\theta(x,y_w)\big)\,\big(\nabla\log\pi(y_w\mid x) - \nabla\log\pi(y_l\mid x)\big) \right], \]

with \(\hat r_\theta(x,y) = \beta \log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\). Conceptually and practically, why does this make DPO different from (and more stable than) just maximizing \(\log\pi(y_w\mid x)\) and minimizing \(\log\pi(y_l\mid x)\) with a fixed weight?

questions.title: How do sequence length and tokenization affect the log-probability ratios in DPO?
questions.question_body:
DPO uses sequence-level log-probabilities inside the ratio \(\log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\). For autoregressive LMs this sum decomposes over tokens. 
- Does this introduce a length bias (longer \(y\) having larger-magnitude log-probs)? 
- Do implementations normalize by length or use EOS-aware strategies? 
- If \(y_w\) and \(y_l\) differ substantially in length, could that systematically skew the implicit reward \(\hat r_\theta\)?

questions.title: What happens if the reference policy used in DPO differs from the policy that generated the preference data?
questions.question_body:
The paper suggests using \(\pi_{\text{ref}}=\pi^{\text{SFT}}\) (the policy that generated the comparisons) when available, but otherwise proposes fitting a reference by maximizing likelihood on preferred completions \(y_w\).
- How sensitive is DPO to mismatch between the true data-generating policy and the chosen \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)? 
- Is there any bias introduced by training \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) on \(y_w\) only (since that uses preference signal to define the baseline)? 
- Are there diagnostics for when a poor \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) harms learning?

questions.title: Which assumptions are required for Theorem 1 (representing any BT/PL reward class as a log-probability ratio)?
questions.question_body:
The paper states that, under mild assumptions, any reward class consistent with Bradley–Terry/Plackett–Luce can be represented as

\[ r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)} \]

for some \(\pi\). What precisely are the assumptions (e.g., support conditions, absolute continuity, function class capacity of \(\pi\), boundedness of rewards)? Do these assumptions hold for finite-vocabulary autoregressive LMs with typical tokenization, and how do degenerate cases (e.g., zero probabilities) fit into the theorem?

questions.title: How does the control-as-inference view lead to the actor-critic objective with the normalization term?
questions.question_body:
The paper rewrites minimizing \(\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_\theta\,\Vert\,\pi^*)\) as maximizing an expectation of

\[ f(r_\phi,\pi_{\text{ref}},\beta) - \beta \log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}, \]

where

\[ f(r_\phi,\pi_{\text{ref}},\beta) = r_\phi(x,y) - \beta\log \sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\exp(\tfrac{1}{\beta}r_\phi(x,y)). \]

Could someone derive this step-by-step and clarify the interpretation of the second term in \(f\) as a "soft value function" or baseline? How exactly does omitting this term increase variance in policy gradient, and why does DPO’s reparameterization avoid needing a learned value baseline?

questions.title: Why does the logistic weighting in DPO’s gradient stabilize training compared to naive unlikelihood?
questions.question_body:
The gradient for a single pair is weighted by \(\sigma(\hat r_\theta(x,y_l)-\hat r_\theta(x,y_w))\), which is large when the model currently prefers the wrong response. Intuitively this seems like an adaptive hard-example mining. Can someone explain: 
- How this weighting prevents the degeneration observed with a fixed-weight unlikelihood objective? 
- Whether this can be seen as a form of importance weighting or margin maximization? 
- Are there conditions where this weighting might still lead to mode collapse or overconfidence?

questions.title: What is the exact DPO loss for Plackett–Luce rankings with more than two candidates?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions an extension from Bradley–Terry (pairwise) to Plackett–Luce (rankings). For a ranked list \(y_{(1)} \succ y_{(2)} \succ \dots \succ y_{(k)}\), what is the explicit DPO objective in terms of the policy/reference log-probability ratios? Is it equivalent to summing pairwise BT-style losses over all adjacent pairs, or does the PL-specific factorization yield a different (preferably lower-variance) estimator?

questions.title: How robust is DPO to violations of the Bradley–Terry assumption (e.g., intransitivities or annotator noise)?
questions.question_body:
Bradley–Terry assumes that pairwise preferences arise from differences of a latent scalar reward. Real human preferences may have intransitivities or context effects. 
- If the data violate BT, does DPO converge to a well-defined optimum (e.g., the best logistic-probit fit)? 
- Are there diagnostics or regularizers to deal with noisy or inconsistent labels? 
- Would a different preference model (e.g., Thurstone/Case V) drop-in replace BT in DPO, and if so, what changes in the loss?

questions.title: How to handle numerical stability when \(\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\) is extremely small or zero?
questions.question_body: The DPO loss uses ratios \(\log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\). In practice, if \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) assigns tiny probability to a completion (or zero due to truncation), this log-ratio can explode. What are recommended safeguards: adding \(\epsilon\), clipping log-probs, restricting to overlapping support, or smoothing \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\)? How do these choices interact with the theoretical guarantees?

questions.title: Does DPO require on-policy sampling like PPO, or is it fully off-policy with a fixed dataset?
questions.question_body:
The DPO objective is an expectation over a fixed dataset of preference pairs \(\mathcal{D}=\{(x,y_w,y_l)\}\). 
- Is DPO unbiased even if \(\mathcal{D}\) was collected from \(\pi^{\text{SFT}}\) rather than the evolving \(\pi_\theta\)? 
- Are there any off-policy corrections needed (e.g., importance sampling) if the distribution of \(x\) or \(y\) under \(\pi_\theta\) drifts far from \(\mathcal{D}\)? 
- How does this compare to PPO’s need to sample from the current policy during training?

questions.title: How does DPO resolve the reward identifiability issue, and what does the normalization constraint mean?
questions.question_body:
Rewards in BT/PL are only identifiable up to adding a function of the context \(f(x)\). The paper says DPO selects a canonical representative via

\[ \sum_y \pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\,\exp\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\beta} r(x,y)\right) = 1, \]

which makes \(\pi(y\mid x)\) a valid distribution. Could someone explain: 
- Why this particular constraint picks out a unique representative in each equivalence class, and 
- How this is related to the partition function of the optimal policy in the KL-regularized RL objective?

questions.title: Why does DPO not require sampling from \(\pi_\theta\) during training if the original RL objective involves \(\mathbb{E}_{y\sim \pi_\theta}\)?
questions.question_body:
The RL objective is

\[ \max_{\pi_\theta} \; \mathbb{E}_{y\sim \pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}[r(x,y)] - \beta\,\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi_\theta\,\Vert\,\pi_{\text{ref}}). \]

Yet DPO optimizes a binary cross-entropy over a fixed preference dataset without sampling from \(\pi_\theta\). Intuitively I see the change-of-variables argument, but can someone make it precise: in what sense are we still optimizing the same underlying objective, and why does this not introduce on-policy sampling requirements?

questions.title: Is the KL reported in evaluation the same KL that DPO implicitly regularizes during training?
questions.question_body:
The paper reports sequence-level \(\mathbb{D}_{\text{KL}}(\pi\,\Vert\,\pi_{\text{ref}})\) on held-out prompts. DPO’s loss contains the ratio \(\log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\) but not an explicit KL expectation term. 
- Are we guaranteed that varying \(\beta\) in DPO will trace out different points on the same reward/KL frontier as PPO? 
- In practice, how closely does DPO’s implicit control of KL match the measured KL under different decoding temperatures?

questions.title: How should I interpret decoding temperature at evaluation time given a KL constraint during training?
questions.question_body:
DPO trains a policy under a KL constraint to \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\) (via \(\beta\)). At evaluation, samples are drawn with a temperature parameter that scales logits. 
- Does changing temperature effectively alter the KL at inference in a predictable way? 
- If so, is there a principled way to pick temperature that preserves the intended KL-regularization or reward/KL tradeoff learned during training?

questions.title: How does DPO’s implicit baseline compare to PPO’s value-function baseline in terms of variance?
questions.question_body: PPO uses a learned value function or reward normalization (e.g., subtracting a baseline) to reduce variance, while DPO’s reparameterization leads to a loss without explicit baseline learning. Can someone compare the variance properties of the DPO gradient estimator vs. PPO’s policy gradient with a learned baseline, and explain why DPO tends to be more stable in practice on language tasks?

questions.title: How should I fairly compare DPO to Best-of-\(N\), given Best-of-\(N\) uses a separate reward model at inference?
questions.question_body: The paper compares DPO with Best-of-\(N\), which samples \(N\) candidates and picks the best under a learned reward. Since Best-of-\(N\) offloads optimization to test-time selection using a reward model, while DPO learns a single policy, are they even optimizing the same target? How should I interpret a higher win rate for DPO vs. Best-of-\(N\): is it due to better reward alignment, better generalization of the policy, or differences in the reward model quality?

questions.title: Is DPO equivalent to logistic regression on features given by log-probability ratios? If not, what breaks the analogy?
questions.question_body:
For pairwise preferences, the DPO likelihood is

\[ \log \sigma\!\left( \beta\log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_w\mid x)} - \beta\log \tfrac{\pi_{\theta}(y_l\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y_l\mid x)} \right). \]

This looks like logistic regression where the "feature" for example \((x,y)\) is \(\log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}\) and the "weight" is \(\beta\). But the feature depends on \(\theta\) itself, so it’s not a standard convex logistic regression. What are the optimization implications—e.g., non-convexity, local minima—and are there known tricks that help convergence (curriculum, initialization, ratio clipping)?
